newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa in rudderless drift, says opposition.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa in rudderless drift, says opposition.

text.p: South Africa's opposition National Party sounded an alarm bell for 1997 on Tuesday, accusing President Nelson Mandela's government of steadily losing its grip on the country.
Citing a checklist of what it termed government failures, the party warned that South Africans would soon experience enormous disappointment with the Mandela government.

"The impression of a ship drifting downstream, apparently rudderless, is constantly compounded," party leader and ex-president F.W. de Klerk said in an advance text of his New Year's message to South Africans.
He said the government had failed to keep its promises on education, health, reconstruction and development and privatisation, which did not meet targets in 1996.
He also cited "the bungling of foreign affairs and, above all, the surging crime wave".

South Africa stunned Taiwan in November by announcing it would break off relations with the island republic in favour of mainland China -- overriding frequent promises to stand by Taiwan. Critics said recognising Beijing displayed realism, but they questioned why South Africa still insisted on close ties with Cuba, Libya and Iran.

And local corporations throughout 1996 warned that violent crime such as vehicle hijacking and armed robbery was getting out of control and was becoming a serious deterrent to foreign investment in the country.

The white-led National Party quit South Africa's national unity coalition government in May, citing irreconcilable differences over the country's new constitution -- since pased into law -- but also confidence that the new democracy was ready for a vigorous parliamentary opposition.

De Klerk said the plunge in the value of the rand, which lost 30 percent of its value against the dollar in 1996, and the continuing loss of "brainpower and experience" inflicted by white emigration were ominous signs.
Mandela's ruling African National Congress (ANC), he charged, "displays a lack of vision for the country and for itself, and it is in the grip of an identity crisis which is harming the country".
"The expectations aroused by President Mandela and the ANC are enormous. Before long, the disappointment will take on the same proportions," de Klerk's message said.
The National Party leader said it was a matter of urgency that South Africa's macro-economic plan be pushed ahead with determination.
"It is imperative that the privatisation of government assets now be taken further, before their value is perhaps diminished by poor management and a variety of compromises," he added.
The National Party was prepared to do its part through political cooperation but also through "fearless criticism", de Klerk pledged.
